notes:
I've put together notes for 21 of the 23 verses. Most of the traditional reading comes from Enduring Word (David Guzik, read in full up to v. 12), John Wesley's Notes, the Geneva Bible notes and Precept Austin. The research has some real gaps. I found nothing from an Orthodox source (oca.org), Bible Odyssey or the NET Bible notes, and nothing distinctly Pentecostal beyond Guzik. I couldn't open the Pulpit Commentary and Barnes pages, so they appear only through search snippets. I didn't get to read Gill or Ellicott for this chapter apart from one Ellicott excerpt on v. 1. Verses 9 and 11 rest only on the Catholic sources, and vv. 16–23 are covered more thinly than the first half.

---

**v. 1**
- **Traditional:** "Continue in sin" is a present-tense verb, so Paul means sin as a habitual way of life, not occasional stumbles. Guzik also cites Rasputin as an extreme example of teaching that more sin brings more grace. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-6/
- Ellicott says the previous chapter might seem to point to an Antinomian conclusion (that grace makes moral law irrelevant). But for the Christian this is impossible, because in principle he is dead to sin. These considerations might seem to lead to an Antinomian conclusion. If the increase of sin has only led to a larger measure of forgiveness it might be thought well to continue in sin, and so to enhance the measure and glory of forgiving grace. But to the Christian this is impossible. In regard to sin he is, in theory and principle, dead. https://biblehub.com/romans/6-1.htm
- Wesley: Paul now defends his teaching against this charge and removes the very foundation of it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/6.htm
- **Debated popular teaching (hyper-grace):** Monergism (Reformed) criticises Joseph Prince. It says he frequently cites Romans 5:20, "where sin increased, grace abounded all the more," as a justification for his hyper-grace teaching, without addressing the immediate context in Romans 6. https://www.monergism.com/joseph-prince
- Ligonier (Reformed) describes people who think that once you have grace you can live however you like, and answers them with Paul's "God forbid!" https://learn.ligonier.org/qas/how-should-we-respond-to-the-hyper-grace-movement

**v. 2**
- **Traditional:** Becoming a believer changes our relationship to sin for good. Before, we were dead *in* sin (Eph 2:1); now we are dead *to* sin. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-6/
- Wesley defines "dead to sin" as freed both from the guilt and from the power of it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/6.htm
- Geneva notes: justification and sanctification always go together. Being "dead to sin" means the power of our natural corruption has been removed. https://www.ccel.org/g/geneva/notes/Romans/6.html
- Piper (Baptist): the question is rhetorical. It is really a statement: We can't live in sin if we died to it. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/are-we-to-continue-in-sin-that-grace-might-increase
- GotQuestions: this does not mean believers are sinless, only that sin is no longer their master. https://www.gotquestions.org/continue-in-sin-that-grace-may-abound.html

**vv. 3–4** (the traditions differ most here, over baptism)
- **Traditional/evangelical:** "Baptized" means immersed or covered over. Guzik calls water baptism a dramatization of the believer's identification with Christ. It illustrates the spiritual reality but does not bring it about. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-6/
- **Baptist:** MacArthur reads vv. 3–4 as a spiritual union with Christ, and says there's no water in Romans 6. https://www.gty.org/sermons/80-370/believers-baptism
- Piper treats v. 4 as what water baptism portrays. He argues that immersion fits the burial imagery: Nobody stays under the water of baptism. We come up out of the water. After death comes new life. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/what-baptism-portrays
- Precept Austin: a person dies to sin through faith, before water baptism. It calls "baptismal regeneration" (the belief that baptism itself brings new birth) a tragic error. https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_64-7
- GotQuestions says the same: baptism symbolizes what has already happened. https://www.gotquestions.org/baptism-salvation.html
- **Reformed:** Ligonier, citing the Westminster Confession, says baptism actually confers divine grace, albeit only to those to whom the grace "belongs"—the elect. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/baptism-and-union-christ
- Geneva notes call baptism "a sign and pledge" of the death, burial and resurrection of the believer with Christ. https://www.ccel.org/g/geneva/notes/Romans/6.html
- **Lutheran:** The LCMS lists Romans 6:3–4 among passages where Jesus promises that this does something. It uses Luther's arguments to defend infant baptism and to oppose rebaptism. https://resources.lcms.org/reading-study/concerning-rebaptism-for-christians/
- **Methodist:** Wesley takes a middle position: In baptism we, through faith, are ingrafted into Christ. He sees an allusion in v. 4 to the ancient practice of baptism by immersion. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/6.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary** (snippet only): Paul is pointing back to the time of their baptism. These passages describe adult baptism, so they cannot fairly be pressed as applicable in all respects to infant baptism. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/romans-6.html
- **Catholic:** Aquinas cites v. 3 and v. 11 and concludes that by Baptism man dies unto the oldness of sin, and begins to live unto the newness of grace. https://www.newadvent.org/summa/4069.htm
- Catholic Answers replies directly to the "no water" argument and calls the sacramental reading the most natural one. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/what-good-is-water-baptism

**v. 5**
- **Traditional:** "United together" describes a very close union, which Morris compares to a graft growing into a tree. Sharing Christ's death makes sharing his resurrection certain. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-6/
- Wesley: the two go together. Those conformed to his death will also know the power of his resurrection. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/6.htm
- Geneva notes: no one who goes on living in sin is sanctified. They add that we grow daily but will never be perfectly sanctified, as long as we live here. https://www.ccel.org/g/geneva/notes/Romans/6.html

**v. 6** (Protestants differ on how complete this death is)
- **Traditional/evangelical:** The death of the "old man" is a settled fact that God accomplished. Our part is to count it as done. Guzik separates the old man from the "flesh", which explains why believers still feel sin's pull. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-6/
- Precept Austin teaches the same distinction and rejects the view that a believer has two active natures. https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_66-7
- **Methodist/Wesleyan:** Wesley reads it as a process. The old man is crucified with Christ, mortified, gradually killed, by virtue of our union with him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/6.htm
- **Reformed (Geneva):** "Body of sin" means That wickedness which remains in us. https://www.ccel.org/g/geneva/notes/Romans/6.html
- **Catholic:** Aquinas quotes a gloss on this verse: "If a man after Baptism live in the flesh, he has concupiscence to fight against, and to conquer by God's help." https://www.newadvent.org/summa/4069.htm
- Catholic Answers: baptism erases original sin, but the leftover inclination to evil (concupiscence) remains and summon[s] him to spiritual battle. https://www.catholic.com/qa/concupiscence-and-original-sin

**v. 7**
- Wesley: the one who has died with Christ is freed from the guilt of past sin and the power of present sin, as dead men are freed from their former masters. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/6.htm
- Guzik: slavery to sin can only be broken by death. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-6/
- Some translations render the verse "justified from sin", for example the Catholic Public Domain Version. https://biblehub.com/cpdv/romans/6.htm

**v. 8**
- Wesley: "dead with Christ" means Conformed to his death, by dying to sin. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/6.htm
- **Catholic:** Aquinas cites this verse to argue that baptism incorporates a person into Christ's passion and death. https://www.newadvent.org/summa/4069.htm

**v. 9**
- The only reading I found was Aquinas's, under v. 3–4. Wesley gives no note on this verse.

**v. 10**
- Wesley: Christ died to sin To atone for and abolish it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/6.htm
- Geneva: "once" means once for all. https://www.ccel.org/g/geneva/notes/Romans/6.html
- Guzik: the new life is given so that we live to please God, not ourselves. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-6/
- Precept Austin: Christ died *unto* sin as well as *for* it, breaking its power. https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_64-7

**v. 11**
- Guzik: "reckon" is an accounting word. We are never told to crucify the old man, only to count him already dead. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-6/
- Precept Austin sums up vv. 6–13 in three steps: know (v. 6), consider (v. 11), present (v. 13). https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_66-7

**v. 12**
- Wesley: the body must be subject to death, but it need not be subject to sin. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/6.htm
- Geneva: Paul is urging the believer to strive against corruption. "Reign" means sin's unchallenged rule. https://www.ccel.org/g/geneva/notes/Romans/6.html
- Guzik: only someone already set free can be told "do not let sin reign." Many Christians never experience this freedom because of unbelief, self-reliance or ignorance. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-6/

**v. 13**
- Guzik: walking in freedom takes two steps. First, stop presenting your members to sin. Second, enlist them positively in God's service. He illustrates with a freed prisoner who still lives like a prisoner. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-6/
- Wesley: sin is a "mere tyrant"; God is our "lawful King." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/6.htm

**v. 14**
- Wesley: "under law" is a dispensation that shows sin without enabling victory over it. Grace brings complete victory to those under the Spirit's influence. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/6.htm
- Geneva: sin is not yet extinct in us, but victory is promised to those who contend bravely. https://www.ccel.org/g/geneva/notes/Romans/6.html
- Guzik: this is a promise that sin will not have *dominion*, not that it will be absent before glory. He quotes Bruce: "To treat being *under grace* as an excuse for sinning is a sign that one is not really *under grace* at all." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-6/

**v. 15**
- Wuest, quoted by Precept Austin: the first question (v. 1) was about habitual sin. This one is about occasional, planned acts of sin. Paul answers by showing that the Christian has changed masters. https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_615-20
- BibleHub commentary: grace rescues from sin's penalty and breaks its power. https://biblehub.com/romans/6-15.htm

**v. 16**
- Pulpit (snippet): two incompatible services are contrasted. Sin leads to death; obedience leads to righteousness. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/romans-6.html

**v. 17**
- Wesley: "form of doctrine" literally means a mould. Our minds should take the shape of the gospel as liquid metal takes the shape of its mould. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/6.htm
- Geneva makes the same "mould" point. https://www.ccel.org/g/geneva/notes/Romans/6.html
- Pulpit (snippet) corrects the King James wording to "whereunto ye were delivered." https://studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/romans-6.html

**v. 18**
- Wesley sets out Paul's argument so far as a sequence: bondage, then law, then faith, then justification, then the Spirit, then free service of righteousness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/6.htm
- Geneva: by nature we are slaves to sin; by grace we become servants of righteousness. https://www.ccel.org/g/geneva/notes/Romans/6.html

**v. 19**
- Wesley: "righteousness" means conformity to God's will, and "holiness" means conformity to the whole divine nature. Servants of righteousness go on to holiness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/6.htm

**v. 20**
- Wesley: in all reason, believers should now be as zealous serving God as they once were serving the devil. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/6.htm
- Geneva: "free from righteousness" means righteousness had no rule over you. https://www.ccel.org/g/geneva/notes/Romans/6.html

**v. 21**
- Geneva: Paul sets the opposite results of sin and righteousness side by side. "End" means the reward or payment. https://www.ccel.org/g/geneva/notes/Romans/6.html

**v. 22**
- Piper (Baptist) draws out that eternal life is presented as the outcome of sanctification: being freed from sin and enslaved to God. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/are-we-to-continue-in-sin-that-grace-might-increase
- Barnes (snippet): "everlasting life" here is the counterpart of "death" in v. 21. He argues this shows the death meant is eternal punishment, not physical death. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/romans-6.html

**v. 23**
- Wesley: "death" means temporal, spiritual and eternal death. Evil works earn their wages; good works do not, because eternal life is a free gift. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/6.htm
- Geneva: death is the punishment due to sin, but we are sanctified freely to everlasting life. https://www.ccel.org/g/geneva/notes/Romans/6.html
- Barnes (snippet): eternal life is the mere gift and mercy of God, and the contrast shows that one is as lasting as the other. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/romans-6.html
